memory_update.text: NNI should be treated as the cleanest public education-finance infrastructure reference name for this node because it combines student-loan servicing, payment technology, and tuition-management exposure, but later layers must separate fee-based servicing from balance-sheet net interest income.

MMS/Aidvantage is a direct federal student-loan servicing contractor and belongs in the reference lane, but materiality is uncertain because student-loan servicing is embedded in broader government-services operations.

FLYW is an underfollowed education affordability/payment-rail candidate because its university receivables, payment-plan, 529, sponsor invoicing, and cross-border tuition workflows sit one step away from student-loan demand.

BFAM/EdAssist is a hidden employer-benefits administration candidate; exposure is likely less pure than FLYW or NNI, but it maps to employer tuition assistance and student-loan repayment benefit administration.

Navient should remain as a watchlist/negative-control name rather than a top Layer 1B candidate for now: it is public and historically tied to education-loan servicing, but federal servicing exit, CFPB settlement/bans, and legacy credit exposure may dominate the infrastructure thesis.

For this node, the best Serenity chokepoint evidence will be contract durability, servicing account volumes, compliance workload, payment-plan adoption, university ERP integration depth, and employer-benefit administration growth—not loan origination volume alone.

node: Student finance, loan servicing, repayment administration, and affordability infrastructure
summary: Layer 1B expansion for the student-finance servicing node found four US-listed companies with plausible direct exposure to student-loan servicing, education payments, tuition-management, or employer education-benefit administration. The reference lane is anchored by Nelnet and Maximus/Aidvantage, which directly touch federal or education-focused loan servicing infrastructure. The underfollowed lane highlights Flywire as a higher-education payment and receivables workflow platform, and Bright Horizons as a less obvious employer tuition-assistance and student-loan-benefit administrator through EdAssist. This pass intentionally avoids balance-sheet-heavy private student lenders unless servicing or administration is the core exposure; Navient remains a watchlist/negative-control name because federal servicing exit and regulatory settlement risk may overwhelm the infrastructure thesis.
